issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: For a police trauma profile, the trigger set is not clinically coherent as a group. Physical touch can fit, but crash imagery and burnt smell together suggest a road traffic accident or fire-related trauma rather than police-related trauma, and there is no supporting memory or appraisal content tying these cues back to police trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. It more commonly fits sexual assault or severe physical violation. Here it is unsupported by the trigger and memory items, which focus on fragmented recall and guilt rather than shame/violation themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance towards dangerous people could occur after police trauma, but in this profile it is weakly supported because the triggers point toward accident/fire cues rather than interpersonal threat cues. This creates a cross-node mismatch between maladaptive strategy content and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination/feeling dirty' is more typically coherent with sexual assault or severe bodily violation trauma. In a police-trauma profile, it is hard to reconcile this appraisal unless there are other items indicating sexualized assault, humiliating bodily violation, or related memory content, which are absent here.

A tactile trigger of general physical touch would usually imply trauma involving bodily contact/restraint. That could occur in police trauma, but in this profile there is no supporting memory or appraisal content about physical restraint, assault, or contact-based threat. Given the rest of the profile emphasizes authority/police cues, danger, mistrust, and guilt, this broad touch trigger stands out as insufficiently supported and clinically hard to place.

vignette: Vikram had always worn his consulting blazer with pride as a civilian liaison for the city's community safety initiative, but on that sweltering July afternoon, the uniform meant something entirely different. He had been walking alongside Sergeant Miller, a man whose steady demeanor had earned Vikram's complete trust. When a report of a disturbance led them into a cramped alley, the air suddenly turned thick with the acrid scent of burning insulation from a nearby wiring fault. That immediate olfactory danger cue yanked him straight into the memory of the incident, stripping away the years and leaving him trapped in the exact second the situation fractured. Before he could speak, Miller had drawn his weapon, mistaking a dropped tool for a threat. Vikram tried to step forward, but he knew exactly what had unfolded and yet was utterly unable to find words to describe it. What he remembered most vividly was the intense guilt on recall, sharp and unrelenting, as he watched the sudden, brutal scramble of boots and shouted commands that followed. Over the months that followed, his belief that the world was a dangerous place and that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted began to warp how he recalled those final moments. He stopped seeing the alley as a misjudgment and started viewing it through a lens of absolute peril, convinced that any authority presence could instantly turn lethal. This pervasive mistrust of people meant that his nervous system became hypersensitive to the very cues that had sparked the original trauma. He caught himself scanning every street corner, his eyes locking onto people in uniform long before he consciously registered why they frightened him. Even the faintest whiff of a burnt smell from a passing delivery truck or a restaurant back alley would send his pulse racing, his negative appraisal that authority was inherently untrustworthy directly fueling his acute sensitivity to these everyday triggers. The guilt on recall and his inability to explain clearly what happened became the engine for his daily survival tactics. Determined to never be caught off guard again, Vikram began rehearsing conversations meticulously before any interaction, running scripts in his head for weeks just to navigate a simple grocery trip or a client call. He stopped making any plans for the future, paralyzing himself with the fear that unexpected events would invite the same catastrophic betrayal. At his graphic design firm, this hypervigilance towards people manifested as an exhausting, constant scan of the studio. He would sit at his drafting table, staring at the monitors of a logo project, while his gaze continually darted to the door, checking for authority figures, his attention fractured long before he could focus on the work. What he did was not passive; it actively sustained the trauma network. The hours spent rehearsing conversations and the weeks of avoided future plans prevented his mind from processing the event naturally, leaving the original memory raw and unrefined. Every time he retreated into silence to avoid explaining clearly, the guilt on recall only deepened, as if his silence were a confession of complicity. This cycle of avoidance directly fed his negative appraisals, teaching his brain that staying rigid and withdrawn was the only way to maintain safety. By continuously scanning for dangerous people, he convinced himself that the world remained fundamentally hostile, and the very act of avoiding plans reinforced his conviction that people could not be trusted to keep him safe. Consequently, his maladaptive strategies became a magnifying glass for his triggers. The more he hypervigilized his environment, the more pronounced the uniform and olfactory cues became, until they dominated his perception of reality. His wife, Anaya, noticed how he would abruptly shut down when the news mentioned a police raid, his face draining of color as the olfactory danger cue of the memory overrode his present reality. What finally drove him to sit in my office was a quiet collapse at work. He had lost the thread while trying to explain a missed deadline to his supervisor, his rehearsed scripts failing him entirely. He was here hoping to break the loop that had stolen his voice and his future, terrified that without intervention, he would remain trapped in a world where danger waited behind every door, every uniform, every familiar scent.
